newsitem.title: EGYPT: Libyan vigilantes unleashed on businessmen.
newsitem.headline: Libyan vigilantes unleashed on businessmen.

text.p: Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi has unleashed a new wave of economic vigilantes to stamp out what he says is profiteering and corruption, travellers from Libya said on Tuesday.

The vigilantes, young men in groups known as "volcano" committees, have raided hundreds of shops in Libyan cities, confiscating goods and money on the grounds the shopkeepers were charging more than official prices, they said.

Authorities working with the vigilantes have rounded up thousands of Libyan businessmen, including goldsmiths and farm and factory owners, and taken them to Tajoura prison, 20 km (12 miles) east of the capital Tripoli, they added.
The campaign has made food hard to find in some areas and stimulated a black market, they said.
The activities of the committees appear to be an escalation of a "purification" campaign Gaddafi launched in June against smuggling and other economic crimes.

Diplomats in Tripoli and the Libyan opposition in exile said in September the campaign was an attempt by Gaddafi to appease popular discontent at economic hardship and remove possible opponents among the nouveaux riches.
Phone calls to several diplomats in Tripoli on Tuesday were cut as soon as someone spoke the words "shops" or "committees".

The travellers, who declined to be named for their safety when they return, said "volcano" committees were composed of poor urban youngsters who receive no pay but live off the pickings from their raids.
Many Libyan civil servants have not received salaries for up to six months and some military officers have taken to driving taxis in Tripoli and Benghazi to make ends meet, they said.
"The aim of the campaign is to distract Libyan public opinion from the political situation, with the noticeable appearance of Islamist groups," one Libyan merchant said.

He said young members of the Revolutionary Committees, the ideological movement Gaddafi created, were planning trials of members of the executive on corruption charges. The trials would be televised, as on several previous occasions, he added.
Since 1992 Libya has been under limited U.N. sanctions, including a ban on flights in or out of the country, but these do not affect oil exports, the main source of foreign currency.

Diplomats say the main reason for hardship is more than 25 years of mismanagement, an uncertain climate for private-sector activity and the diversion of state revenues to massive projects of dubious economic benefit.
